edits.name: Research agent extra readers: read-only browser behind an action firewall hook, and summarize CLI
edits.description: The research helper can also read public pages that need JavaScript, logged out, and pull the text out of long articles, videos and podcasts. An in-house hook keeps the browser read-only in code (one profile, no typing, no form filling, no uploads, no page scripts); bot walls and logins stop it.
edits.example: Jordan texts: "What does the rec centre page say about spring swim lessons?" The page shows nothing without JavaScript, so research opens it in the logged-out browser and her own agent relays the dates with the link. Or Tony texts a link to a 40-minute video and asks for the main points.
edits.how: Two readers, on the research agent only. (1) The `browser` tool on the managed `openclaw` profile, with `headless: true` on that profile and `browser.evaluateEnabled: false`. Four switches come first: `browser.enabled` (off since M0), the browser tool on research's sandbox tool allow list (it is on the sandbox default deny list), the per-agent tool allow, and a place for the browser to live. First choice is the roadmap's sandbox browser container with the LAN blocked; its image has to be built from a source checkout because the npm install does not include the Dockerfile. The fallback is the host's managed profile through `sandbox.browser.allowHostControl` and an explicit host target, which the docs say to keep off for sandboxed agents unless you trust them. (2) A host stdio MCP that wraps `summarize --extract --json` and returns extracted text from articles, YouTube and podcasts without calling a model; the wrapper pins `--firecrawl off`, holds no third-party keys and checks the address itself. The firewall (formerly WEB-03): an in-house plugin with `api.on("before_tool_call", handler, { matcher: ["browser"] })`, default-deny and failing closed. It rejects any `profile`, `target` or `node` other than the one assigned to the agent (a missing profile is filled in or blocked, because an omitted profile means the default one) and rejects `systemProfile`, `into`, `domains` and `dashboard`. Of the tool's 24 actions it allows only a listed read-only subset (for example status, tabs, open, navigate, focus, close, snapshot, text, screenshot). `act` and `upload` are not on that list in this build, which blocks every act kind at once: `batch`, `evaluate`, `press`, `clickCoords`, `drag`, `wait`, `resize`, `type`, `fill`, `select` and `click`. If a page later proves unreadable without scrolling, `act` comes back only for kinds on an allowlist of its own (`scrollIntoView`, `hover`), each with an eval case. The hook reads the URL from `targetUrl` first and `url` second, looks inside a nested `request` object, and blocks any call whose top-level and nested kinds differ. Unknown agent, missing field, unknown action or kind, or a parse error returns a block; the runner itself blocks the call if the handler throws or times out. Research reads the open web, so there is no site allowlist here; navigation stays http and https under the WEB-01 private-network block. Not built here: the exact-hostname allowlist and the ask-a-parent-before-typing approval branch, whose only consumer is the roadmap's M6 jobs agent.

caveats: Bot walls, logins, CAPTCHAs and two-factor prompts stop it. The bundled browser skill tells the agent to report them as manual steps, and the docs say sandboxed browser sessions are more likely to be flagged as bots.

The sandbox browser image cannot be built from the npm install; it needs a source checkout. The host alternative needs allowHostControl, which the docs say to keep off for sandboxed agents unless you trust them.

The hook sees tool parameters, not page meaning: a click carries a snapshot ref, not the button's label, so code cannot tell 'Next' from 'Submit'. That is why clicks are blocked outright in this read-only build.
A navigation check in a hook sees the URL the agent asked for, not where redirects or page scripts go next; the private-network block in WEB-01 is the backstop.
With open and navigate allowed, a link straight to a file is saved into the managed downloads directory without the download action ever being called.

The parameter names come from the installed 2026.9.7 browser tool schema and can change with any update. Default-deny keeps a new action blocked until someone allows it, but the hook needs a contract test after every OpenClaw update.

summarize runs on the host, outside the SSRF policy that covers web_fetch and the browser, and has its own third-party extraction fallbacks; the wrapper must switch those off and check the address itself.
An independent evaluation on live websites found web agents much less competent than earlier benchmarks suggested, so expect misses on complex pages.
edits.safety: The research agent holds no private data, no memory and no accounts, and this browser is a managed profile with none of the family's signed-in sessions, so an injected page has nothing to steal. What a real browser adds is a way to act, so the limits on profile, target and actions live in code and fail closed, page script evaluation is off in config, and the home network is out of reach (WEB-01). The hook is in-house code on the security boundary: one parsing mistake is a bypass, so it gets its own injection eval cases before the browser is switched on. No profile on this browser ever holds a login, and CAPTCHAs are reported, never solved.

edits.name: Talk mode on Tony's iPhone (native speech loop, operator only)
edits.description: Tony installs the OpenClaw iPhone app and holds a spoken back-and-forth with his own agent: the phone transcribes, the gateway answers as it would a text, and the reply is spoken. The app also adds a Listen action on any reply and a Siri phrase or Action Button shortcut that starts voice. It is Tony's phone only: the app is a full gateway client and a device node, and nothing verified today can hold a second adult's phone to her own agent.
edits.how: The App Store OpenClaw app on Tony's iPhone, the same install and pairing as the iPhone app entry (OCL-01), reaching the gateway over the tailnet (the app connects over LAN or tailnet; this gateway is Tailscale Serve only). Before pairing (limits folded in from VOX-03): the phone command ceiling is in place (device commands denied first; OCL-01, formerly HOM-08); `talk.agentId` is set explicitly and names a memory-less agent, because it is one value for the whole gateway and receives every Talk session that arrives without an agent-prefixed key; `tts.modelOverrides.allowProvider` stays off (its default) so a reply directive cannot move speech to a cloud provider; and the operator's inspect script gains a read-only listing of paired devices and their scopes. Tony generates the pairing code with `openclaw qr --limited` instead of the default admin handoff. `--voice-node` is not for this phone: it drops the write scope, so typed chat (`chat.send`) and the Listen action (`tts.speak`) stop working, and whether Talk still runs is untested. Native Talk is a loop: Apple Speech recognition on the phone, Gateway chat on the agent picked in the app (tony-main), then `talk.speak` playback. `talk.speak` reads the Talk block, not the `tts` block: set `talk.provider` plus `talk.providers.<id>` to a speech provider (the local engine from VOX-04 can be named there); with no Talk provider the gateway call fails and the docs mention an iPhone system-voice fallback. Other keys: `talk.speechLocale`, `talk.silenceTimeoutMs`, `talk.interruptOnSpeech`. Entry points: the inline Talk control, the `Start Live Voice` App Shortcut, the Siri phrase, or the Action Button.
depends_on: the OpenClaw iPhone app paired on Tony's phone with device commands denied first (OCL-01; this was IPH-01 and HOM-08)
a Talk speech provider under `talk.provider` (the VOX-04 local engine), or accept the iPhone system-voice fallback
decision: is a write-scoped gateway credential on Tony's phone acceptable
a written device-revocation step for a lost phone
a second adult's phone only after gateway.roles is proven with the iOS app on a test device
caveats: Audio can leave the house even in the native loop: the docs say Apple Speech recognition on iOS may use network services. The transcript then goes to OpenAI as text like any typed message.
iOS may suspend background audio, so voice is best-effort unless the app is in the foreground; the Siri shortcut does not bypass unlock or foreground restrictions.
Dictating an iMessage to Happy with the keyboard microphone or Siri already works today with no setup. Talk adds the continuous loop, barge-in and spoken replies, not a new capability.

Everything about the pairing applies here unchanged and is spelled out in the iPhone app entry (OCL-01): the app is a gateway client first, every pairing profile includes operator.read (session lists, chat history, logs and read-only browsing of every agent's workspace), `--limited` removes only operator.admin and leaves write, approvals and Talk secrets, the phone registers as a node, App Store builds use a vendor-hosted push relay, and a lost phone has to be revoked on the gateway. On a second adult's phone the other adult's agent memory would be readable.
`--voice-node` does not rescue the native loop: the chat turn is chat.send, which the docs class as write-scoped, and that profile holds only read and talk.

Talk playback uses the Talk speech provider, not the general tts block. The docs name elevenlabs (cloud), mlx and system for Talk, and the mlx helper ships with the Mac app, which is not installed here; expect the iPhone's own system voice.

`openclaw qr` only advertises a Tailscale URL when OpenClaw itself owns the Serve route (`gateway.tailscale.mode`). The config repo sets it to serve on a loopback bind, so this looks met; confirm on the live gateway. mDNS discovery is off there, so pairing is by QR or setup code.

A phone paired without operator.admin cannot open the app's Settings pages, where this device's Talk, Voice Wake, background-listening and speakerphone switches live. Plan on the inline Talk control in Chat and the Start Live Voice shortcut.
There is no speaker identification anywhere in the stack: whoever is near the microphone is the user.
edits.safety: Tony's phone only. That is acceptable because section 1b of the roadmap already makes Tony the control-plane owner who can read everything; pair with the limited profile, keep the node surface unapproved, and treat the phone as an admin-adjacent credential. A second adult's phone has no safe placement today: the docs describe operator scopes as a guardrail inside one trusted operator domain, not a boundary between people, and the named-roles feature that could limit her to her own agent rejects the device and bootstrap tokens that QR pairing issues. Voice input is the speaker's own words, so no untrusted-content leg is added to tony-main, and tool policy, hooks and the family-only recipient pin still apply to the agent's tool calls. A child must not use this Talk session: every agent is cloud-backed and Apple Speech on iOS may send audio to Apple.
unverified: Whether Talk still runs on an iPhone paired with a `--voice-node` code. What is certain from the installed scope table is that such a phone loses typed chat and the Listen action (chat.send and tts.speak need the write scope).
